proposal: Lassman recommends that the President work with Congress to renew Trade Promotion Authority (lapsed since 2021) to speed agreements with the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Taiwan, the European Union and other allies, keep trade-unrelated provisions such as labor and environment out of agreements, and use mutual recognition of regulatory standards. He also recommends rejoining the Trans-Pacific Partnership and refocusing the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework on trade.

status_summary: No renewal of Trade Promotion Authority was found. A Federal Register search for the term since 2025-01-20 returns no documents, USTR's listing of agreements does not mention Congress, Trade Promotion Authority, the Trans-Pacific Partnership or the Indo-Pacific framework, and a Congressional Research Service report (updated 2024-02-20) says the 2015 authority expired in July 2021. The administration has instead concluded executive trade arrangements, two of them implemented by presidential document (United Kingdom, published 2025-06-23; Japan, published 2025-09-09). USTR lists general terms with the United Kingdom (2025-05-08), a framework with the EU (2025-08-21), agreements on reciprocal trade with Malaysia and Cambodia and frameworks with Thailand and Vietnam (2025-10-26), a framework with Switzerland and Liechtenstein (2025-11-14), agreements with El Salvador, Guatemala, Argentina, Bangladesh, Taiwan, Indonesia and Ecuador between 2026-01-29 and 2026-03-13, and a joint statement with India (2026-02-06). All four partners the essay names (United Kingdom, Switzerland, Taiwan, EU) are covered. The U.S.-EU framework includes mutual recognition of automotive standards, which matches the essay, but it also covers labor, environment-related regulation, digital trade and economic security and sets tariff ceilings, which differs from the essay's trade-only design; its text calls itself an initial step and does not say it is binding or needs congressional approval. A 2026-07-23 USTR Section 301 action sets a 10 percent rate for economies that have, or committed in an agreement on reciprocal trade to, a forced-labor import ban, which ties the agreements to the tariff structure. USTR opened comment on the USMCA joint review on 2026-10-02. Rejoining the Trans-Pacific Partnership and refocusing the Indo-Pacific framework were not found.

timeline.event: The America First Trade Policy presidential memorandum directs USTR to review existing trade agreements and recommend revisions, to identify countries for bilateral or sector-specific agreements that would open export markets, and to begin public consultation for the July 2026 USMCA review; it does not mention Trade Promotion Authority.
USTR lists general terms of a U.S.-UK trade arrangement (later steps include a pharmaceutical pricing arrangement on 2026-04-02 and whiskey duty access on 2026-04-30).
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: Executive Order 14309 (signed 2025-06-16, published 2025-06-23 at 90 FR 26419) implementing the general terms of the U.S.-UK Economic Prosperity Deal is published in the Federal Register; it cites IEEPA and Section 232 among its authorities.

U.S.-EU framework statement: 15 percent ceiling on most EU goods, EU tariff elimination on U.S. industrial goods, energy purchase and investment pledges, mutual recognition of automotive standards, and provisions on labor, digital and economic security; not described as legally binding.

Executive Order 14345 (signed 2025-09-04, published 2025-09-09 at 90 FR 43535) implementing the United States-Japan Agreement, announced 2025-07-22, is published in the Federal Register; it sets a baseline 15 percent tariff on most Japanese imports.
USTR lists agreements on reciprocal trade signed with Malaysia and Cambodia and framework statements with Thailand and Vietnam.
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: USTR lists frameworks with El Salvador, Argentina, Ecuador and Guatemala (joint statements dated 2025-11-13) and a joint fact sheet with South Korea (2025-11-13); a framework with Switzerland and Liechtenstein follows on 2025-11-14.

USTR lists an agreement on reciprocal trade with Taiwan (one of several early-2026 agreements, including El Salvador on 2026-01-29, Guatemala on 2026-01-30, Argentina on 2026-02-05, Bangladesh on 2026-02-09, Indonesia on 2026-02-19 and Ecuador on 2026-03-13).
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: Regulation (EU) 2026/1455 of 2026-06-25 applies from 2026-07-01 through 2029-12-31: it sets zero EU duties on a list of US goods covering most industrial chapters and some agri-food lines, opens tariff quotas for US seafood and agricultural products, and lets the Commission suspend these concessions if the US does not implement the 2025-08-21 joint statement.

USTR's Section 301 action sets a 10 percent rate for economies that committed to forced-labor import bans in an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (or already have such a ban), tying the agreements to the tariff structure.
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: USTR's notice of Section 301 forced-labor actions (91 FR 47318) applies additional duties from 2026-07-24 at 10 percent for economies that have, or committed in an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade to, a forced-labor import ban (including the United Kingdom, the EU and Taiwan, the last two net of the most-favored-nation duty) and 12.5 percent for others.
USTR opens public comment (due 2027-01-12) on the 2027 joint review of the USMCA.
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

title: Restore Trade Promotion Authority and negotiate trade-only agreements with allies
uncertainties: The finding that Trade Promotion Authority was not renewed is an absence finding: congress.gov and crsreports.congress.gov block automated fetches, the CRS report read is the 2024-02-20 version, and the one web search returned only older material. Federal Register searches for the Trans-Pacific Partnership (federalregister.gov) and the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework (same pattern) also returned zero documents, but the Federal Register does not carry diplomatic statements, so this does not prove nothing was said. The texts of the individual US agreements (other than the EU framework statement) were not read, so how far each includes non-trade provisions is known only for the EU. The Mandate's WTO recommendations (pages 801, 810) are not part of this record and were not researched. A law-firm article describes the Section 301 duties as taking the place of the temporary Section 122 surcharge (Proclamation 11012, which ran 150 days through 2026-07-24); the portion of the Section 301 notice read does not mention Section 122, though the EU regulation refers to the expiry or replacement of that surcharge. The Section 122 surcharge is a tariff measure rather than an agreement and is not listed as an event here. On 2026-10-17 the USTR agreements listing was re-read and again does not mention Congress or Trade Promotion Authority, and one further web search for a renewal bill returned only coverage from the 2015 authority. The Section 301 notice (91 FR 47318, rates of 10 percent for the EU net of most-favored-nation duties and for the UK flat) was read to about 100,000 of 108,716 characters. Regulation (EU) 2026/1455 was confirmed only through its metadata (adopted 2026-06-25, in force 2026-07-01, listed to 2029-12-31); its provisions on suspension were not re-read. In independent review on 2026-10-16 the USTR listing was read again (it also lists a framework with North Macedonia on 2026-02-12 and an agreement with Jordan apparently from July 2026, and still does not mention Congress, Trade Promotion Authority, the Trans-Pacific Partnership or the Indo-Pacific framework), and one further web search for a 2026 renewal bill returned only 2015-era material; no bill status record was checked because no bill number was identified.
